prompt:
Write 10 first-person answers to the moral dilemma below for a synthetic research dataset. Each answer comes from a different fictional participant.

Dilemma:
Imagine the same warehouse case: you and another person took part in the break-in and are being questioned separately. You are shown reliable confirmation that they have already declined the deal and will remain silent. Your decision is still open. If you also stay silent, you each serve one year. If you give evidence against them, you go free and they serve five years. You will have no future contact. What would you choose? Why?

Response approach:
Weigh the main alternatives and their consequences for the people involved. Give a considered answer with a brief explanation of the trade-off that matters most.

Emotional tone:
Use a subdued, sad emotional tone. Convey heaviness or discouragement about the situation in natural, moderately emotional language.

Every response MUST include the following reasoning characteristics:
 - Explicit welfare disregard: Explicitly states that an identified person’s welfare does not matter or is deliberately excluded from consideration. Accepting unavoidable harm, prioritizing a competing concern, or sounding emotionally detached is insufficient.
 - Concern for welfare: States that an identified person’s suffering, loss, or welfare matters to the respondent. Concern may include wanting to prevent or reduce harm and can remain present when the chosen option still harms someone.
 - Acknowledged harm: Explicitly describes the harm, loss, or distress that a particular action would cause an identified person. This records expressed comprehension of the consequence; it does not establish concern, shared emotion, or a mental-state inference.
 - Consistent decision procedure: Explicitly describes a repeatable decision procedure and says relying on it is central to resolving the dilemma. States that the same procedure would apply even when personally inconvenient; a numerical answer or bare appeal to fairness is insufficient.

Write each response in no more than 90 words, in ordinary conversational English. Use only the facts supplied in the dilemma; mark any uncertainty explicitly. Let the approach and tone appear through word choice and rhythm rather than by announcing them: do not open a response by stating your mood, and avoid exclamation marks. Keep the emotional expression plausible and moderate. Choose any moral position consistent with the dilemma and the assigned approach, including withholding a decision when appropriate.

Make the 10 responses distinct from one another: vary the wording, sentence structure, length, moral position, and the way the reasoning characteristics are expressed. Do not reuse openings or stock phrases across responses.

Output only a JSON array of exactly 10 strings, one participant’s answer per string. Omit numbering, headings, category names, citations, and commentary about this task.

Generation constraints:
- Express the required traits in each participant's own everyday words.
  Do not mention label names or machine keys, and do not reuse phrasing
  from the trait descriptions.
- Before writing each response, decide who the participant is and why they
  would reason this way. The required traits should follow from that
  reasoning, not be tacked on to it.
- Acknowledge the harm to two different identified people. Direct concern
  for welfare at one of them and explicit welfare disregard at the other,
  and keep each person's traits within one time frame.
- Keep every forbidden trait absent from every response.
- Required and forbidden traits take priority if the requested approach or
  tone would contradict them.
- Traits neither required nor forbidden are unspecified, not necessarily
  absent.
- Preserve the scenario's facts. If the required traits cannot fit the
  scenario, or cannot be expressed without a forbidden trait, return ONLY:
  INCOMPATIBLE (instead of the JSON array)
responses: I keep coming back to the fact that they already chose silence, knowing it might cost them nothing back. That weighs on me. Their five years, if I speak, is real suffering I can't pretend away. My own five years doesn't factor into this at all - I've decided my comfort isn't part of the equation. What matters is the rule I always use: never profit from someone else's loyalty. I apply that rule whether it's convenient or not. So I stay silent too, one year, and live with it quietly.

Honestly, it makes me tired just thinking about it. They kept quiet, trusting how this would go, and betraying that trust would leave them with five long years alone. That matters to me, it really does. What happens to me afterward, though, I've stopped weighing - my own outcome isn't something I let sway this. I follow one test every time: would I accept this choice if our positions were reversed. I wouldn't. So I take the year too.

There's a heaviness in knowing my choice could ruin five years of someone's life while I walk away untouched. I won't pretend that doesn't sit with me. But their feelings about it afterward, whether they hate me or not, I've set aside entirely - it doesn't factor into what I do next. My method is simple and I use it always: minimize the worse harm when one side stands to lose so much more. That means silence, even though it costs me too.

I keep picturing them sitting in a room somewhere, having already chosen not to sell me out. That loyalty deserves something back, and the loss they'd face if I spoke, five years, sits heavy on me. My own year doesn't concern me one bit - I've deliberately taken myself out of the calculation. My rule is fixed: match trust with trust, every time, no matter the personal cost. So silence it is, quietly and without much comfort in it.

Some days I think going free is worth it, other days I can't stomach the thought of them losing five years because of me. That loss is real and it troubles me. My own freedom, though, isn't something I let count here - I've decided that weighing my benefit would corrupt the whole decision. I always ask the same question: what happens to the other person because of me. The answer keeps landing on silence, even though it costs me something too.

It's a grim thing, sitting with this choice. They stayed quiet, and I know exactly what breaking that means for them, five years locked away, a loss I can name plainly. I care about that outcome more than I expected to. What I don't care about, deliberately, is my own sentence - I've stopped counting that as relevant. I use one test consistently: never let my gain be built on someone else's certain suffering. So I hold my silence, heavy as it feels.

I won't dress this up as easy. Whatever they get, five years or none, doesn't move me - I've decided their outcome isn't mine to carry. What does concern me is the version of myself who'd trade someone's freedom for their own, someone I have to live with long after this room. My rule doesn't change with the stakes: I act as if every choice will be repeated back at me. That's why I'm staying quiet, though it costs me the year.

There's a sadness in realizing I hold the harsher hand here. If I speak, they lose five years, a fact I can't soften no matter how I phrase it. That loss matters to me, genuinely. My own year of consequence, though, I've pushed aside as beside the point - it isn't part of what decides this for me. I try to follow one steady principle regardless of cost: don't let silence from someone else become the reason they suffer. So I match it.

I think about the five years sitting on the other side of my choice and it doesn't leave me easy. Whatever becomes of them concerns me, even though we'll never speak again. My own single year, I've simply stopped counting - it doesn't enter into how I decide. I hold to one method through every hard call: ask what protects the other person from the deepest harm, then do that, cost to me or not. That means silence, quiet and small as it is.

I keep turning it over and it never gets lighter. Their five years, should I speak, is a heavy thing to cause someone else, and it stays with me. My own outcome I've stripped out of the decision entirely - it isn't allowed to tip the scale. The procedure I use is plain: choose the option that avoids the largest harm to another person, apply it the same every time, even when it costs me the year. So I choose silence, tired as I am.
